summary.text: London dispersion forces are a type of intermolecular force that acts between atoms and molecules that are normally electrically symmetric.
They are part of the van der Waals forces and are the weakest of the intermolecular forces.
Their effects are most obvious in very non-polar systems such as hydrocarbons, where they are enough to condense a gas into a liquid or solid.

facts.label: First explanation
facts.value: Fritz London, in 1930, for noble gas atoms

facts.label: Size and strength
facts.value: Larger, heavier molecules show stronger dispersion forces

facts.label: Halogens at room temperature
facts.value: Fluorine and chlorine gases, bromine liquid, iodine solid

items.prompt: Going from fluorine to chlorine to bromine to iodine, a substance at room temperature changes from gas to liquid to solid. Which change in dispersion forces fits?

options.label: They get stronger as the molecules get larger
They get weaker as the molecules get larger
They stay the same, as only the bonds differ
They switch off once a substance turns solid

items.explain: Larger and heavier molecules show stronger dispersion forces, a trend shown by the halogens, which run from gases through a liquid to a solid.

items.prompt: A heavy molecule has a large, spread-out electron cloud. Why does that give it stronger dispersion forces?

options.label: A spread-out cloud holds its electrons rigidly in place
Its electrons can be redistributed more easily
Its nucleus carries a permanent charge that pulls neighbours in
Its cloud forms covalent bonds with each neighbouring molecule

items.explain: Larger, more dispersed electron clouds are more polarizable, which means the electrons are more easily redistributed.

items.prompt: Oxygen gas is cooled until it becomes a liquid. Which attraction mainly drives that change?

options.label: Hydrogen bonds between neighbouring oxygen molecules
Ionic attraction between oxygen atoms
Attraction between permanent dipoles in each molecule
Attractive London forces arising from electron motion

items.explain: The liquefaction of oxygen and nitrogen gases is dominated by attractive London dispersion forces.

items.prompt: Two non-polar molecules sit in water instead of in a vacuum. How do the dispersion forces between them typically look?

options.label: Unchanged, since the surrounding medium never matters
Stronger, since water adds extra pull between them
Often less pronounced, since water feels the fluctuations too
Gone entirely, since water cannot be polarized at all

items.explain: In aqueous solutions dispersion effects are frequently less pronounced, because of competition with polarizable solvent molecules.

items.prompt: A chemist wants a sample where London dispersion forces are easiest to see, because few other attractions are present. Which should she pick?

options.label: Table salt, held together by ionic bonds
Water, with a web of strong attractions
Iodine, a highly symmetric non-polar molecule
A liquid whose molecules each carry a permanent dipole

items.explain: The effects are most obvious in very non-polar systems, including highly symmetric molecules like bromine and iodine.

items.prompt: Why did Fritz London call this effect "dispersion"?

options.label: Because the force makes molecules spread apart
Because his theory resembles the quantum theory of light dispersion
Because it was found while studying gases spreading in air
Because it spreads charge evenly around the nucleus

items.explain: The London theory has much similarity to the quantum mechanical theory of light dispersion, which is why London coined the phrase.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: London dispersion forces are attractions between atoms and molecules that are normally electrically symmetric, meaning their electrons are spread evenly around the nucleus. They go by several other names, including London forces and instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. They belong to the wider group of van der Waals forces and are named after the German physicist Fritz London. Of all the intermolecular forces, they are the weakest.

paragraphs.heading: How it works
paragraphs.text: The arrangement of electrons around an atom or molecule changes from moment to moment. Each change creates a brief electric field, which nearby atoms and molecules feel, and their own electrons shift in response. The overall effect is that electron movements in neighbouring atoms become correlated. A full account needs quantum mechanics, but the effect is often pictured as short-lived dipoles forming and attracting one another.

paragraphs.heading: Bigger means stronger
paragraphs.text: Larger, heavier atoms and molecules feel stronger dispersion forces than smaller, lighter ones. The reason is polarizability, a measure of how easily electrons can be redistributed; bigger, more spread-out electron clouds are more polarizable. The halogens show the trend clearly, growing in size from F₂ to Cl₂ to Br₂ to I₂. At room temperature fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.

paragraphs.heading: Weak alone, strong together
paragraphs.text: Between single atoms and molecules the force is quite weak, and it drops off quickly with separation R, as 1/R⁶. In liquids and solids, though, the effect adds up over the whole volume of material, so it can be quite strong and fades much more slowly with distance. Between two bulk solids, for example, the force per unit area falls as 1/R³. In hydrocarbons and waxes, dispersion forces are enough to turn a gas into a liquid or solid, and they also dominate when oxygen and nitrogen gases are liquefied.

paragraphs.heading: Inside water
paragraphs.text: When a third substance, rather than empty space, separates the particles, the situation gets more complicated. In water, dispersion effects are often less marked, since polarizable solvent molecules compete. A fluctuation in one molecule is felt both by the surrounding water and by other molecules.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: In 1930 Fritz London was the first to explain why noble gas atoms attract each other, using a quantum-mechanical theory built on perturbation theory. The popular picture of two interacting instantaneous dipoles was invented after he had worked out the proper theory. London chose the phrase dispersion effect because his theory has much in common with the quantum theory of light dispersion. In physics, dispersion means a quantity varying with frequency; here, that frequency belongs to the fluctuating electrons.
